The AudioDome at Western University in London, Ontario, is a dome of loudspeakers that uses ambisonic rendering to place a sound source anywhere around a listener at its center. Ambisonics promises hearing researchers controlled experiments in the complex, dynamic soundscapes our hearing evolved for. But known reconstruction errors could affect how people perceive where a sound is and what it is. In The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, Nima Zargarnezhad’s team reports testing the system’s limits before using it with human listeners.

The results were encouraging. Human spatial acuity is high in front of us and drops toward the sides of the head, and listeners in the AudioDome showed a very similar pattern, suggesting that the array reproduces sound locations at a finer scale than human perception can resolve. Accuracy and precision did not depend on how far a simulated source lay from an actual loudspeaker, so the spatial resolution holds almost anywhere in 3D space.

The limit lies in frequency. The algorithm reproduced sound energy accurately only up to about 4 kHz, enough for speech, though it sounds somewhat degraded, like a telephone call. Errors at higher frequencies distorted elevation cues, so sources with high-frequency content were heard at unexpected heights. Overall, the authors conclude, ambisonics can reproduce the identity and location of many common sounds, including speech, at least as finely as human spatial acuity. Applications range from VR and AR to car audio, hearing research and music production.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “Simulate sound in 3D at a finer scale than humans can perceive,” a 2025 news release from AIP Publishing. Read the original.
